Last time we found that a black hole cannot shine brighter than its Eddington
luminosity for long, and so it cannot swallow gas faster than its Eddington
rate — and that both limits grow in proportion to its mass. That last fact has
a surprising consequence. A black hole that is allowed to eat faster the bigger
it gets does not grow steadily. It grows exponentially, like money earning
compound interest. **This lecture finds how fast a black hole can possibly
grow, why a more efficient black hole grows more slowly, and why the most
distant quasars force us to ask what black holes start out as.**

## What actually crosses the horizon

In astrophysics, we are often dealing with things that involve many complex
processes at once. One way to deal with that is to consider bottlenecks in the
processes, and timescales are good for that. We are going to find out how fast
a black hole can possibly grow.

Recall from [lecture 8](../eddington-limit/index.qmd#the-eddington-accretion-rate)
that a black hole accreting as fast as it is allowed has an accretion
luminosity equal to its Eddington luminosity:

$$
\eta\, \dot M c^2 = \frac{4\pi G c\, m_p M_{\mathrm{BH}}}{\sigma_T} .
$$ {#eq-at-limit}

Recall that $\eta$ is the fraction of the mass-energy coming in that goes into
radiation.

:::: {.callout-tip title="Ask yourself"}
What actually crosses the horizon?

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
**The rest of it!** A fraction $1 - \eta$ of the mass that falls in.
:::
::::

The energy that leaves as light came out of the mass of the gas, so it is mass
the black hole never gets. The black hole grows only by what is left:

$$
\dot M_{\mathrm{BH}} = (1 - \eta)\, \dot M .
$$ {#eq-mdot-bh}

Up to now we have used $\dot M$ for the rate at which gas flows in toward the
black hole, without asking how much of it the black hole keeps. Here we have to
ask, because we are considering how much is leaving the system, which is
important when a significant amount of mass-energy is being radiated away.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-crosses}

1. A black hole is fed gas at $1\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$.

   a. If its radiative efficiency is 10%, how fast does its own mass grow?
   b. How fast if it is spinning as fast as possible, with an efficiency of
      42%?
   c. In part (a), what becomes of the mass that does not cross the horizon?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   **(a)** $0.9\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$. **(b)**
   $0.58\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$. **(c)** It leaves as light. The
   $0.1\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$ of rest mass energy is the trillion Suns'
   worth of luminosity we found in lecture 7's worked example.
   :::

2. In lecture 8 we found that a $10^{9}\,M_\odot$ black hole with a radiative
   efficiency of 10% can accrete at most about
   $22\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$. How fast can its own mass grow?

:::

## Growing at the Eddington limit

::: {.panel-tabset .tracks}

### Physical intuition

The key is in @eq-at-limit: the fastest a black hole may be fed is proportional
to its mass. Double the mass and you double the allowed feeding rate. So a
black hole growing at its limit always gains the same *fraction* of its mass in
the same time, whether it is ten Suns or a billion.

That is exactly how money grows in a bank account that pays a fixed rate of
interest. The interest each year is a fixed fraction of what is already in the
account, so the more you have, the more you gain, and the balance grows faster
and faster. Anything that grows by a fixed fraction of itself grows
**exponentially**.

For a black hole the clock is called the **Salpeter time**, $t_{\mathrm{S}}$:
in each Salpeter time the mass grows by a factor of $e \approx 2.718$. For the
standard efficiency of 10% it is about 50 million years. That sounds slow, but
it compounds. In ten Salpeter times the mass grows by a factor of $e^{10}$,
about 22,000; in twenty, by about 500 million.[It is named for Edwin Salpeter,
whose 1964 paper on gas accreting onto massive objects [@salpeter1964] was
among the first to argue that quasars are powered this
way.]{.aside .content-visible when-format="html"}

### Mathematical explanation

Start from the Eddington accretion rate of lecture 8 and divide both sides by
the mass. That gives the fastest rate at which a black hole can take in gas,
as a fraction of its own mass:

$$
\dot m \equiv \frac{\dot M}{M} < \frac{4\pi G m_p}{\eta\, c\, \sigma_T} .
$$ {#eq-mdot-norm}

The right-hand side is the same for every black hole with the same efficiency,
because the mass has gone. It has units of one over time, and its inverse,
$\eta\, c\, \sigma_T / 4\pi G m_p$, is about 45 million years for
$\eta = 0.1$: the time it would take a black hole to swallow its own mass at
its current limit.

Now let the black hole keep only $1 - \eta$ of that, as in @eq-mdot-bh. We can
substitute in our expression for $\dot M$ and explicitly include the time
derivatives to get this first-order ordinary differential equation:

$$
\frac{dM_{\mathrm{BH}}}{dt}
  = \frac{4\pi (1 - \eta)}{\eta}\, \frac{m_p G}{c\, \sigma_T}\, M_{\mathrm{BH}} .
$$ {#eq-growth}

So we have an equation of the form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx} = a\, y
$$

for some constant $a$. That's an exponential solution!

$$
M_{\mathrm{BH}} = M_0 \exp\left[\frac{t}{t_{\mathrm{S}}}\right] ,
$$ {#eq-exp}

for some initial mass $M_0$, and where the Salpeter time is

$$
t_{\mathrm{S}} = \frac{\eta}{4\pi (1 - \eta)}\, \frac{c\, \sigma_T}{m_p G} .
$$ {#eq-salpeter}

This timescale is called an **e-folding** timescale because it is the time
that it takes for the mass to grow by a factor of $e$.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Check that the exponential solves the growth equation"}
Differentiate @eq-exp with respect to time. The derivative of
$e^{t/t_{\mathrm{S}}}$ is $e^{t/t_{\mathrm{S}}}/t_{\mathrm{S}}$, so

$$
\frac{dM_{\mathrm{BH}}}{dt}
  = \frac{M_0}{t_{\mathrm{S}}} \exp\left[\frac{t}{t_{\mathrm{S}}}\right]
  = \frac{M_{\mathrm{BH}}}{t_{\mathrm{S}}} .
$$

That is @eq-growth, as long as $1/t_{\mathrm{S}}$ is the constant in front of
$M_{\mathrm{BH}}$ there — which is exactly how @eq-salpeter defines it. And at
$t = 0$ the exponential is 1, so the mass starts out at $M_0$, as it should.
:::

The units of $c\, \sigma_T / m_p G$ are $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} \times
\mathrm{cm^2} = \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$ on top and $\mathrm{g} \times
\mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}} = \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-2}}$ on the bottom, which
leaves $\mathrm{s}$; the efficiency is a pure number. *Do the units make
sense?* A timescale is a time, so yes. Put in the numbers:

$$
t_{\mathrm{S}} \approx 450\ \mathrm{Myr} \times \frac{\eta}{1 - \eta} ,
$$ {#eq-salpeter-num}

where a Myr is a million years. For the standard efficiency of 10% that is
50 Myr.

### Numerical exploration

Here is @eq-exp for a $10\,M_\odot$ seed growing at its limit for 500 million
years, at several efficiencies.

```{python}
#| label: growth-ladder

import math

c = 2.99792456e10     # cm s^-1
G = 6.6732e-8         # cm^3 g^-1 s^-2
m_p = 1.6726e-24      # g
sigma_T = 6.6524e-25  # cm^2
Myr = 3.156e13        # s

etas = [0.057, 0.1, 0.2, 0.42]
M_0 = 10     # seed mass in M_sun
t = 500      # growing time in Myr

K = c * sigma_T / (4 * math.pi * m_p * G) / Myr
print(f"seed {M_0} M_sun, growing for {t} Myr")
fmt = "{:>6} {:>9} {:>9} {:>10}"
print(fmt.format("eta", "t_S", "doubling", "final M"))
print(fmt.format("", "(Myr)", "(Myr)", "(M_sun)"))
for eta in etas:
    t_S = K * eta / (1 - eta)
    M = M_0 * math.exp(t / t_S)
    print(f"{eta:6.3f} {t_S:9.1f}",
          f"{t_S * math.log(2):9.1f} {M:10.2e}")
```

:::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: from ten Suns to a billion"}
**The question.** How long does it take a $10\,M_\odot$ black hole to grow to
$10^{9}\,M_\odot$, if it accretes at its Eddington limit the whole time with a
radiative efficiency of 10%?

First the Salpeter time. It needs the ratio $c\, \sigma_T / m_p G$ from
@eq-salpeter. Substitute into its top and its bottom with the units attached,
and no arithmetic yet:

$$
\begin{aligned}
c\, \sigma_T &= \left(3.00 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)
  \left(6.65 \times 10^{-25}\ \mathrm{cm^2}\right) \\
m_p G &= \left(1.67 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g}\right)
  \left(6.67 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The top carries $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} \times \mathrm{cm^2} =
\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$ and the bottom $\mathrm{g} \times
\mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}} = \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-2}}$. The cubic
centimeters cancel, and $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ divided by $\mathrm{s^{-2}}$ leaves
$\mathrm{s}$. *Do the units make sense?* We are after a time, so yes.

$$
\frac{c\, \sigma_T}{m_p G}
  = \frac{1.995 \times 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}}
         {1.114 \times 10^{-31}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-2}}}
  = 1.79 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{s}
$$

The efficiency is a pure number, so

$$
t_{\mathrm{S}} = \frac{0.1}{4\pi\, (0.9)} \times 1.79 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{s}
  = 1.58 \times 10^{15}\ \mathrm{s} ,
$$

and in millions of years, with the conversion fractions arranged so the
seconds and the years cancel,

$$
\begin{aligned}
t_{\mathrm{S}} &= 1.58 \times 10^{15}\ \mathrm{s}
  \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{yr}}{3.156 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}} \\[0.8em]
  &\qquad \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{Myr}}{10^{6}\ \mathrm{yr}}
  = 50.2\ \mathrm{Myr} ,
\end{aligned}
$$

which is the 50 Myr of @eq-salpeter-num.

Next, solve @eq-exp for the time: divide both sides by $M_0$ and take the
natural logarithm of both sides.

$$
t = t_{\mathrm{S}} \ln\left(\frac{M_{\mathrm{BH}}}{M_0}\right)
$$

The mass ratio is a pure number, because the solar masses cancel, and the
logarithm of a pure number is a pure number. So $t$ comes out in the units of
$t_{\mathrm{S}}$:

$$
\frac{M_{\mathrm{BH}}}{M_0} = \frac{10^{9}\,M_\odot}{10\,M_\odot} = 10^{8}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
t &= 50.2\ \mathrm{Myr} \times \ln\left(10^{8}\right)
   = 50.2\ \mathrm{Myr} \times 18.4 \\[0.8em]
  &= 924\ \mathrm{Myr} \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{Gyr}}{1000\ \mathrm{Myr}}
   = 0.92\ \mathrm{Gyr}
\end{aligned}
$$

where a Gyr is a billion years. Almost a billion years, even growing as fast as
it is allowed the whole time. Doubling from ten Suns to twenty takes exactly as
long as doubling from half a billion Suns to a billion, so most of that time is
spent while the black hole is still small.
::::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## Why efficiency slows growth

It is clearly important to know $\eta$, then, because it sets the timescale for
how fast a black hole can grow. Remember that $\eta$ is the *radiative*
efficiency.

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Decide whether a black hole grows faster with a high efficiency or a low one"}
**Low.** The efficiency appears twice in @eq-salpeter, and both times it slows
the black hole down.

The first is the $1 - \eta$ of @eq-mdot-bh. The efficiency is how efficiently
radiation is created, and $1 - \eta$ is how efficiently matter falls onto the
horizon. A more efficient black hole sends more of what it eats back out as
light and keeps less of it. Going from a non-spinning black hole to a maximally
spinning one, the fraction it keeps falls from 94% to 58%.

The second, and by far the bigger, is the $\eta$ on top, and it comes from the
Eddington limit. The luminosity a black hole may reach is fixed by its mass
alone, whatever its efficiency. A more efficient black hole reaches that
luminosity on less gas, so it is allowed less gas — the nuance we met in
[lecture 8](../eddington-limit/index.qmd#the-eddington-accretion-rate). Going
from an efficiency of 5.7% to 42% cuts the allowed accretion rate by a factor
of 7.4.

Together they make the Salpeter time of a maximally spinning black hole about
12 times longer than that of a non-spinning one.
:::

The major criterion for radiative efficiency is spin, as we saw in
[lecture 7](../accretion-efficiency/index.qmd#where-falling-stops-paying-the-isco),
so spin sets how fast a black hole can grow. Put lecture 7's efficiencies into
@eq-salpeter-num:

| spin | $\eta$ | $t_{\mathrm{S}}$ | doubling time |
|---|---|---|---|
| $a_* = -1$ | 3.8% | 18 Myr | 12 Myr |
| $a_* = 0$ | 5.7% | 27 Myr | 19 Myr |
| typical, spin unknown | 10% | 50 Myr | 35 Myr |
| $a_* = +1$ | 42% | 330 Myr | 230 Myr |

So the property that makes a spinning black hole the most efficient engine we
know of also makes it the slowest-growing black hole. Over a few hundred
million years the difference is enormous (@fig-growth).

```{python}
#| label: fig-growth
#| fig-cap: "The same $10\\,M_\\odot$ seed, formed 186 million years after the Big Bang, growing at its Eddington limit with three different radiative efficiencies. The least efficient black hole grows fastest: at 5.7% its mass grows tenfold about every 63 million years, while at 42% it has grown to only about 46 Suns by the time the other reaches a billion. The star marks the quasar J0313−1806 of the next section; even the fastest of the three reaches that mass, at the open circle, 16 million years too late."
#| fig-alt: "A graph of black hole mass in solar masses, on a logarithmic axis from 1 to 100 billion, against the age of the Universe in billions of years, from 0.15 to 0.8. Three curves start together at a dot marking a 10 solar mass seed at 0.186 billion years. A solid blue curve for a non-spinning black hole with 5.7 percent efficiency rises steeply as a straight line, passing a billion solar masses at about 0.69 billion years. A dashed green curve for 10 percent efficiency rises about half as steeply, reaching only a few hundred thousand solar masses by 0.69 billion years. A dash-dot orange curve for maximal spin with 42 percent efficiency is nearly flat, reaching less than a hundred solar masses by the right edge. A black star at 0.686 billion years and 1.6 billion solar masses, labeled J0313 minus 1806, sits just above the blue curve, with a dotted vertical line beneath it. A short horizontal line runs from the star to an open circle slightly to its right, where the blue curve reaches the same mass, labeled reaches it 16 Myr late."
#| fig-height: 4.03

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.03))

c, G, m_p, sigma_T = 2.99792456e10, 6.6732e-8, 1.6726e-24, 6.6524e-25
Myr = 3.156e13
K = c * sigma_T / (4 * np.pi * m_p * G) / Myr   # in Myr

t_seed, M_seed = 0.186, 10.0      # Gyr, M_sun
t_q, M_q = 0.686, 1.6e9           # J0313-1806
t = np.linspace(t_seed, 0.80, 600)

for eta, color, style, label in (
        (1 - np.sqrt(8 / 9), BLUE, "-", r"not spinning, $\eta = 5.7\%$"),
        (0.10, AQUA, "--", r"$\eta = 10\%$"),
        (1 - np.sqrt(1 / 3), ORANGE, "-.", r"maximal spin, $\eta = 42\%$")):
    t_S = K * eta / (1 - eta)
    M = M_seed * np.exp((t - t_seed) * 1e3 / t_S)
    ax.semilogy(t, np.where(M < 1e11, M, np.nan), color=color,
                linestyle=style, linewidth=2.4, label=label, zorder=3)

ax.plot([t_seed], [M_seed], marker="o", color=INK, markeredgecolor=SURFACE,
        linestyle="none", zorder=4)
ax.annotate(r"seed, $10\,M_\odot$", xy=(t_seed, M_seed), xytext=(8, -14),
            textcoords="offset points", color=INK2, fontsize=10)

ax.axvline(t_q, ymax=np.log10(M_q) / 11, color=MUTED, linestyle=":",
           linewidth=1.2, zorder=2)
ax.plot([t_q], [M_q], marker="*", markersize=17, color=INK,
        markeredgecolor=SURFACE, linestyle="none", zorder=5)
ax.annotate("J0313−1806", xy=(t_q, M_q), xytext=(-12, 6),
            textcoords="offset points", ha="right", color=INK, fontsize=10)

# Where the fastest (non-spinning) line reaches the quasar's mass: 16 Myr late.
eta0 = 1 - np.sqrt(8 / 9)
t_cross = t_seed + K * eta0 / (1 - eta0) * np.log(M_q / M_seed) / 1e3
ax.plot([t_q, t_cross], [M_q, M_q], color=INK, linewidth=1.2, zorder=4)
ax.plot([t_cross], [M_q], marker="o", markersize=6, color=SURFACE,
        markeredgecolor=INK, markeredgewidth=1.4, linestyle="none", zorder=5)
ax.annotate("reaches it\n16 Myr late", xy=(t_cross, M_q), xytext=(8, -30),
            textcoords="offset points", ha="left", color=INK2, fontsize=10)

ax.set_xlabel("age of the Universe  (billions of years)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"black hole mass  ($M_\odot$)")
ax.set_xlim(0.15, 0.80)
ax.set_ylim(1, 1e11)
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
plt.show()
```

   $10^{9}$ years.

   a. What is its final mass if its radiative efficiency is 10%?
   b. What is its final mass if its radiative efficiency is 42%, as for a
      maximally spinning black hole? Explain in one or two sentences why this
      answer is lower than the one in part (a).

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   **(a)** About $4.7 \times 10^{10}\,M_\odot$, twenty Salpeter times. If you

   exponential magnifies small rounding. **(b)** About
   $2 \times 10^{3}\,M_\odot$.
   :::

2. Two black holes grow at their Eddington limits for 300 million years. One is
   not spinning, with $\eta = 5.7\%$; the other spins as fast as possible, with
   $\eta = 42\%$. By what factor does each one's mass grow? Check your answers
   with the Turn the knobs cell.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The non-spinning one by about $6 \times 10^{4}$; the spinning one by about
   2.5.
   :::

## A billion Suns in half a billion years

Some of the most distant quasars — brightly shining accreting black holes — are
already enormous. The quasar J0313−1806 is at a redshift of $z = 7.642$, which
means that we see it as it was 0.686 billion years after the beginning of the
Universe. One measurement of its mass puts it at
$1.6 \times 10^{9}\,M_\odot$.[Its discovery and its mass are reported
in @wang2021.]{.aside .content-visible when-format="html"}

We have reasons to think that the first "seed" black holes formed at about
$z = 20$, when the Universe was 0.186 billion years old. So how small can this
black hole have started, if it grew as fast as it is allowed to?

:::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: the smallest possible seed for J0313−1806"}
**The question.** J0313−1806 had a mass of $1.6 \times 10^{9}\,M_\odot$ when
the Universe was 0.686 billion years old. If its seed formed when the Universe
was 0.186 billion years old and grew at its Eddington limit the whole time,
with a radiative efficiency of 10%, what is the smallest mass the seed can have
had?

The black hole had

$$
\begin{aligned}
t &= 0.686\ \mathrm{Gyr} - 0.186\ \mathrm{Gyr} = 0.500\ \mathrm{Gyr} \\[0.8em]
  &= 0.500\ \mathrm{Gyr} \times \frac{1000\ \mathrm{Myr}}{1\ \mathrm{Gyr}}
   = 500\ \mathrm{Myr}
\end{aligned}
$$

to grow. Solve @eq-exp for the seed mass by multiplying both sides by
$\exp\left[-t/t_{\mathrm{S}}\right]$:

$$
M_0 = M_{\mathrm{BH}} \exp\left[-\frac{t}{t_{\mathrm{S}}}\right]
$$

The exponent must be a pure number. Substitute with the units attached, using
$t_{\mathrm{S}} = 50\ \mathrm{Myr}$ from @eq-salpeter-num:

$$
\frac{t}{t_{\mathrm{S}}} = \frac{500\ \mathrm{Myr}}{50\ \mathrm{Myr}}
$$

The millions of years cancel. *Do the units make sense?* An exponent has to be
a pure number, and this is one, so yes.

$$
\begin{aligned}
M_0 &= 1.6 \times 10^{9}\,M_\odot \times e^{-10.0} \\[0.8em]
    &= 1.6 \times 10^{9}\,M_\odot \times 4.5 \times 10^{-5}
     = 7.3 \times 10^{4}\,M_\odot
\end{aligned}
$$

A seed of at least seventy thousand Suns — not the ten or so Suns of a black
hole left behind by a dying star. And that is the most generous case, with the
black hole accreting at exactly its limit, without a break, for half a billion
years.
::::

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
{{< include ../../in_class/lec09/exercises00.qmd >}}
:::

Starting from a seed of ten Suns, even a non-spinning black hole, the fastest
grower in @fig-growth, reaches this mass 16 million years too late. Only the
least efficient black holes grow fast enough to have a chance at all, and the
least efficient black holes are the ones that spin slowly, or against the
direction their gas orbits.

**Rapid black hole growth requires low spin. Is that okay?** We will leave that
as an open question.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-quasar}

1. Suppose that J0313−1806's seed formed later, when the Universe was
   0.300 billion years old. With the same assumptions as the worked example,
   what is the smallest it can have been?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   About $7 \times 10^{5}\,M_\odot$, ten times heavier for starting
   114 million years later.
   :::

2. The worked example assumed that the black hole grew at exactly its Eddington
   limit, without a break, for the whole 500 Myr. Name two ways a real black
   hole could fall short of that, and say which way each one moves the smallest
   possible seed mass.

:::

## Where the seeds come from

If the biggest black holes cannot be grown in time from the black holes that
stars leave behind, then they must have started from something bigger, or grown
faster than the Eddington limit allows. What a supermassive black hole started
from is called its **seed**, and there are three main ideas for where seeds
come from.

1. **Light seeds: the remnants of the first stars.** The first generation of
   stars, called Population III stars, formed from hydrogen and helium alone
   and are thought to have been very massive. When they died they could have
   left black holes of about $10^{2}\,M_\odot$.
2. **The collapse of a dense star cluster.** In the crowded center of a young
   galaxy, stars can collide and merge with one another, building up a single
   very massive object that collapses to a black hole of about
   $10^{3}\,M_\odot$.
3. **Heavy seeds: direct collapse.** A huge cloud of gas collapses all at once
   into a single supermassive star, or a "quasi-star", which leaves behind a
   black hole of about $10^{5}\,M_\odot$ and skips the small-black-hole stage
   entirely.

Light seeds are theoretically easy to form, but how do they grow fast enough?
Perhaps they grow faster than the Eddington limit for a while. Heavy seeds are
more challenging theoretically: how does a cloud that massive avoid breaking
into smaller parts early on? Maybe that only happens in rare cases.

This is where the Salpeter time earns its keep. At the Eddington limit and an
efficiency of 10%, the time needed to grow from each kind of seed to
J0313−1806's $1.6 \times 10^{9}\,M_\odot$ is

| seed | seed mass | e-foldings needed | time needed |
|---|---|---|---|
| light | $10^{2}\,M_\odot$ | 16.6 | 831 Myr |
| star cluster | $10^{3}\,M_\odot$ | 14.3 | 716 Myr |
| heavy | $10^{5}\,M_\odot$ | 9.7 | 485 Myr |

and only 500 Myr was available. At that efficiency, only a heavy seed makes it.
A light seed would need a lower efficiency — a black hole spinning slowly — or
to grow faster than the Eddington limit for a while.

How would we tell which idea is right? The smallest galaxies host the smallest
black holes, which must be closer to the seed mass, and may tell us the
dominant seeding mechanism. If seeds are light and common, nearly every galaxy,
however small, should have a black hole, and the smallest galaxies should have
small ones. If seeds are heavy and rare, many small galaxies should have no
black hole at all, and the ones that do should have black holes no smaller than
the seeds (@fig-seeding).[This way of posing the question follows the review
by @greene2020.]{.aside .content-visible when-format="html"}

```{python}
#| label: fig-seeding
#| fig-cap: "What the smallest galaxies could tell us about seeds, in a schematic simplified from Greene et al. (2020); the shapes are the point, not the exact numbers. (a) If seeds are light (solid blue), nearly every galaxy has a central black hole; if they are heavy and rare (dashed orange), many small galaxies have none. (b) Light seeds let black holes scale down with their galaxies, while heavy seeds leave the smallest galaxies with black holes no lighter than the seed."
#| fig-alt: "Two schematic panels side by side, each with galaxy mass on a logarithmic horizontal axis from ten million to one hundred billion solar masses. Panel (a) plots the fraction of galaxies with a central black hole, from 0 to 1. A solid blue line for light seeds stays close to 1 at every galaxy mass, dipping only to about 0.9 for the smallest galaxies. A dashed orange line for heavy seeds rises in an S shape from near zero at the smallest galaxies to nearly 1 for galaxies above about ten billion solar masses, always staying below the blue line. Panel (b) plots black hole mass on a logarithmic axis from a thousand to one hundred million solar masses. A solid blue line for light seeds is straight and rises steadily, black hole mass growing in proportion to galaxy mass. A dashed orange line for heavy seeds follows the blue line for large galaxies but levels off at about one hundred thousand solar masses for small galaxies, staying above the blue line there."
#| fig-height: 2.9

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.5, 2.9))
fig.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.42)

M_gal = np.logspace(7, 11, 300)
x = np.log10(M_gal)

ax1.plot(M_gal, 0.9 + 0.1 / (1 + np.exp(-(x - 8.0))), color=BLUE,
         label="light seeds")
ax1.plot(M_gal, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-2.2 * (x - 8.8))), color=ORANGE,
         linestyle="--", label="heavy seeds")
ax1.set_xscale("log")
ax1.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
ax1.set_xlabel(r"galaxy mass  ($M_\odot$)")
ax1.set_ylabel("fraction with a black hole")
ax1.set_title("(a)", loc="left")
ax1.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=10)

light = 1e-3 * M_gal
heavy = np.sqrt(light**2 + 1e5**2)
ax2.loglog(M_gal, light, color=BLUE)
ax2.loglog(M_gal, heavy, color=ORANGE, linestyle="--")
ax2.set_ylim(1e3, 1e8)
ax2.set_xlabel(r"galaxy mass  ($M_\odot$)")
ax2.set_ylabel(r"black hole mass  ($M_\odot$)")
ax2.set_title("(b)", loc="left")
plt.show()
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-seeds}

1. What are the three main ideas for how the seeds of supermassive black holes
   formed? For each of the three, give a one- or two-sentence description of
   the idea.

2. Suppose a $100\,M_\odot$ light seed forms when the Universe is 0.186 billion
   years old and grows at *twice* its Eddington accretion rate, still with a
   radiative efficiency of 10%.

   a. What is its e-folding time?
   b. Could it reach J0313−1806's mass of $1.6 \times 10^{9}\,M_\odot$ by the
      time the Universe is 0.686 billion years old?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
   Doubling the accretion rate doubles the right-hand side of @eq-growth. What
   does that do to the constant in front of $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$, and so to the
   e-folding time?
   :::

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   **(a)** Half the Salpeter time, about 25 Myr. **(b)** Yes. It reaches
   $1.6 \times 10^{9}\,M_\odot$ after about 415 Myr, when the Universe is about
   0.60 billion years old.
   :::

:::

## Summary

| Quantity | Expression | What to remember |
|---|---|---|
| What the black hole keeps | $\dot M_{\mathrm{BH}} = (1-\eta)\,\dot M$ | Mass that leaves as light is mass the black hole never gets |
| Growth at the limit | $dM_{\mathrm{BH}}/dt \propto M_{\mathrm{BH}}$ | The allowed growth rate is proportional to the mass |
| Exponential growth | $M_{\mathrm{BH}} = M_0\, e^{t/t_{\mathrm{S}}}$ | A factor of $e$ every Salpeter time |
| Salpeter time | $t_{\mathrm{S}} \approx 450\ \mathrm{Myr} \times \eta/(1-\eta)$ | About 50 Myr for $\eta = 0.1$ |
| Efficiency and spin | $t_{\mathrm{S}}$ rises with $\eta$ | A spinning black hole grows more slowly: 27 Myr not spinning, 330 Myr at maximal spin |
| Seeds | light $\sim 10^{2}$, cluster $\sim 10^{3}$, heavy $\sim 10^{5}\,M_\odot$ | The earliest quasars need heavy seeds, low spin, or faster-than-Eddington growth |

A black hole growing at its limit grows exponentially, on a clock set by its
radiative efficiency, and that turns a question about the brightest distant
quasars into a question about how black holes begin. We will come back to
seeds when we look more closely at where supermassive black holes come from.
Next time, a different way for black holes to grow and to announce themselves:
merging, and the gravitational waves it makes.
